questions.q: Why can't cloud workload protection be a single uniform product across VMs, containers, and serverless, according to this lesson?
options: Only VMs can be attacked; containers and serverless functions have no meaningful attack surface
Cloud providers deliberately avoid building any workload protection tools
Serverless functions run on the exact same OS layer as VMs, so no distinction is needed
VMs, containers, and serverless functions each expose a genuinely different attack surface, so protection has to be shaped around what can actually go wrong with each
questions.explain: A VM has a persistent OS, a container is built from an inspectable image and often short-lived, and serverless has no reachable OS at all — each needs protection shaped around its actual exposure.

questions.q: What does GuardDuty's Malware Protection for EC2 actually do?
options: It installs a mandatory persistent agent on every EC2 instance
It blocks all outbound network traffic from EC2 instances by default
It performs agentless scanning of attached EBS volumes when GuardDuty suspects malware-related activity
It replaces the need for any vulnerability scanning on EC2 instances
questions.explain: Malware Protection for EC2 is agentless — it scans attached EBS volumes specifically when GuardDuty has reason to suspect malware-related activity, without a persistent agent on the instance.

questions.q: What is the difference between container image scanning and runtime monitoring?
options: Image scanning checks a container image for known-vulnerable packages before deployment; runtime monitoring watches actual behavior while the container is executing
They are two names for the exact same process performed at the same time
Runtime monitoring only applies to Azure, image scanning only applies to AWS
Image scanning happens continuously after deployment and runtime monitoring happens only once before deployment
questions.explain: Image scanning (Defender for Containers/ACR, Amazon Inspector/ECR) is a build-time check; runtime monitoring (the AKS sensor, GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring) catches anomalous behavior a static scan could never see.

questions.q: Why is a tightly scoped, least-privilege IAM execution role described as the highest-leverage control for a Lambda function?
options: Because Lambda functions cannot be scanned for vulnerabilities under any circumstance
Because there is no OS layer to protect in serverless, so the execution role's permissions determine the blast radius if the function's code is ever compromised
Because AWS automatically assigns the correct permissions to every Lambda function with no configuration needed
Because IAM roles have no effect on what a Lambda function can access
questions.explain: With no reachable OS layer, the execution role's scope directly determines how much damage a code-level vulnerability in that function can actually cause.

questions.q: What pattern repeats across VM, container, and serverless workload protection, according to this lesson?
options: All three rely exclusively on a single vendor-neutral agent with no cloud-specific tooling
None of the three require any form of vulnerability assessment

Something checks for known weaknesses before or independent of execution, and something else watches for anomalous behavior during execution — only the source of that "during execution" signal changes
Runtime behavior is never actually monitored in any of the three compute shapes
questions.explain: The lesson's closing pattern: pre-execution vulnerability/image checks pair with during-execution behavioral signal, but that signal's source differs — process telemetry on VMs, audit logs/runtime sensors on containers, network/IAM activity on serverless.
